headline: D.C. Circuit pauses DEA's 29 November medical cannabis trade limit
dek: A 25 November order stays the part of DEA's 30 October letter that bars timely applicants from trading with state-licensed partners outside the federal system.
key_points: The D.C. Circuit on 25 November administratively stayed DEA's 30 October 'Timely Applicant' letter for state-compliant trades with businesses that are neither registrants nor timely applicants.
The court said the pause only buys time to decide the emergency motions and is not a ruling on their merits.
Eight companies told the court on 24 November they faced lost customers, lost revenue and layoffs, citing requests from Trulieve, Curaleaf and Green Thumb for proof of registration.
The 29 November cut-off no longer bites for the trades covered by the order until the court says otherwise; the rest of DEA's letter stands.
body: A federal appeals court has stopped, for now, the Drug Enforcement Administration's plan to cut medical cannabis businesses off from state-licensed partners that sit outside the new federal system. In a one-page order filed on 25 November, a panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit administratively stayed the DEA document known as the 'Medical Marijuana Timely Applicant Information', issued on 30 October, to the extent it governs trades between timely applicants and businesses that are neither federal registrants nor timely applicants.

The order lands four days before the 29 November date on which those trades were due to stop, and two days after the Justice Department asked the court to refuse any stay, as we reported on 24 November. It is temporary by design. The court said the pause gives it time to consider the emergency motions for a stay pending review, and that it 'should not be construed in any way as a ruling on the merits' of those motions.
## What the order says

The order was entered per curiam by Judges Neomi Rao, Justin Walker and Bradley Garcia in Standard Wellness Utah, LLC v. Drug Enforcement Administration, No. 26-1324, which the court has consolidated with Nos. 26-1325 and 26-1329. The respondents are the DEA and its administrator, Terrance Cole. The court's own caption describes the challenged action as the 'DEA-10/30/2026 Letter'.

The stay is narrow and precise. It covers timely applicants' schedule III medical marijuana activities that conform to a state-issued licence and that are conducted with entities that are neither federal registrants nor timely applicants. In plain terms, a business that applied for DEA registration inside the 60-day window can, for the time being, keep buying from and selling to state-licensed partners that missed the window, as long as the deal complies with its state licence.

Nothing else in the 30 October letter is touched. The Marijuana Herald, which first published the order, noted that it does not resolve the underlying challenges or suspend the guidance as a whole. The order also says the stay lasts until further order of the court, not until a fixed date.
> The court has not said the companies are right. It has said the question is serious enough that 29 November should not decide it by default.
## Who asked, and what they told the court

The first petition, filed on 18 November, came from Standard Wellness Utah, Verde Americano of Arizona and NW Confections of Oklahoma. Four Pennsylvania companies filed the second on 19 November, as we reported on 21 November. A third case, No. 26-1329, now sits in the same consolidated group; the order does not name its petitioners and we have not seen that filing.

On 24 November, eight medical cannabis companies filed replies to the government, three of them asking for a ruling by 25 November, according to The Marijuana Herald. The filings put numbers on the harm. PennAlt Organics, a Pennsylvania grower and processor, said it expected to lose about 95% of its third-party customers and might have to lay off all 48 employees. Verde Americano put its exposure at about $600,000 a month, or 40% to 50% of revenue, and said it could lay off about 70% of its 136 staff. Standard Wellness Utah cited about $275,900 a month in sales to medical cannabis pharmacies, and NW Confections warned of possible insolvency.

PennAlt's filing also showed the deadline working through the market before it arrived. It attached emails from Trulieve, Curaleaf and Green Thumb asking for proof of its federal registration status, and the Herald reported that Trulieve and Curaleaf warned they could restrict or suspend business without it. The Pennsylvania companies repeated their claim that DEA staff told manufacturers to wait for a medical marijuana form that was not available until 5 October, more than three months after the window closed.
## The government's position

The Justice Department's case, filed on 23 November, is that the 30 October letter created no new duty. In its reading, the Controlled Substances Act has always required registrants to deal only with other registrants, the April rescheduling order let early applicants operate as if registered while DEA reviews their files, and the letter simply marked the end of a grace period. It also argued the letter is not a final agency action the court can review. A DEA declaration put the number of applications filed in the window at about 7,100: roughly 4,300 for dispensaries, 2,100 for manufacturers and 700 for distributors.

The companies say the letter is a legislative rule issued without notice and comment, contrary to the Attorney General's April order. That dispute is what the panel must now weigh in deciding whether to replace the administrative stay with a stay pending review.
## What it means for operators

For businesses that filed on time, the immediate effect is relief from a hard stop on Sunday. State-compliant supply relationships with partners outside the federal system can continue while the order stands. That matters most in the four states in the litigation, Arizona, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and Utah, which on DEA's own figures account for about 2,800 of the 7,100 early applications.

One open question is reach. The order stays the DEA document itself 'insofar as it relates to Timely Applicants' in general, and does not name the petitioners as the only beneficiaries. On our reading, that language covers timely applicants beyond the companies in court, but the panel has not said so expressly, and operators should not assume a temporary order will hold. The other open question is counterparties. Large multistate operators were already asking smaller suppliers for proof of registration; whether they resume normal ordering will depend on their own risk tolerance, not only on the court.

Two things have not changed. The order does not register anyone, and DEA's view that a federal registration does not permit trades with unregistered businesses is still the government's position in court. Firms that relax their supply chains now could face a different answer if the panel later denies a longer stay.
## What to watch

Watch first for the panel's decision on the emergency motions, which can come at any time and could extend, narrow or end the pause. Watch for any DEA statement on how it will treat transactions made while the administrative stay is in force. The docket also carries routine filing dates running to 21 December and 4 January 2027. Separately, the challenge to the rescheduling order itself, SAM, Inc. v. U.S. Department of Justice, continues before the same court and could reshape the whole framework.
